lines.text: Eleven oh eight at night. Forty seven people are waiting to talk to someone.
Three experts are online. All three are already on a call.
Twelve more are offline, and none of them know any of this is happening.
This is where a two sided marketplace quietly loses money, and most of them cannot see it happen.
Supply is fixed at eighteen sessions an hour. Push demand past that and the queue does not grow. It compounds.
At three times demand, the wait crosses thirty minutes. Yellow.
At five and a half, it is over an hour. Red. By the time tomorrow's report shows it, those customers are gone.
So I built the layer that watches for it.
Delay time and dropout rate are the two triggers. When either one crosses, the system answers on both sides at once.
Prices surge by category. Ten percent on astrology, eighteen on mental health.
And every dollar of that surge is ring fenced. It does not go to margin. It funds the bonus that brings experts back online.
Then the push fires. Tiered, and it names the number of people waiting and what three sessions are worth tonight.
With no incentive, eight percent of experts respond. At sixteen dollars a session, fifty five percent do.
That gap is the entire system.
Without the engine, the queue peaks at sixty five and stays there.
With it, nine experts accept, the delay drops from thirty four minutes to eighteen, and the engine switches itself off.
Four hundred and twenty dollars of surge collected. Three hundred and eighty paid out. The whole response cost the platform forty dollars.
Five modules. Demand signals, health scoring, surge pricing, incentives, and a router that decides what a human actually needs to handle.
One config file. Four marketplace presets.
I built it as a product manager, without an engineering team, because the alternative was watching the queue and doing nothing.
